title: The Promise
full_review:
Director Chen Kaige's epic fantasy romance "The Promise" (Warner Independent) is being touted as the most expensive movie ever made in China, and Kaige puts every yuan (Chinese currency) up on the screen.

Set in China's mythical past, the film tells the story of a beautiful princess, Qingcheng (Cecilia Cheung), whose childhood pact with a goddess to forsake true love for worldly comfort reaps fateful consequences for her and the three rivals vying for her affections: a renowned general, Guangming (Hiroyuki Sanada); his loyal, supernaturally swift slave, Kunlun (Jang Dong-Gun); and a villainous duke, Wuhuan (Nicholas Tse).

Elegiac in tone, the simple plot involves betrayals and mistaken identities in exploring universal themes of honor, self-sacrifice and free will.

A sympathetic Liu Ye plays the most tragic figure, Snow Wolf, a ghostly assassin whose tortured spectral existence illustrates how acquiescence to evil diminishes (in his case, literally) one's humanity.

While exhibiting the same masterful eye for color and composition that he displayed in films like his Academy Award-nominated "Farewell My Concubine" (1993), Kaige's somewhat underwhelming tale of desire and destiny sacrifices character development and narrative clarity in favor of sumptuous visuals and effects-heavy martial arts sequences similar, though inferior, to "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon," "Hero" and "House of Flying Daggers."

Subtitles.

The film contains much stylized action violence, images of battlefield carnage, a massacre scene, a flaming body and a sexual encounter, as well as suggested bathing nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
